title: The King and the Virtuous Wife

keywords: the king and the virtuous wife
full_text:
A powerful king of ancient Persia, while riding through his capital, caught sight of an exceptionally beautiful lady sitting upon the walled balcony of a modest mansion. Enamored by her grace, the king dispatched her husband, who was an officer in the royal guard, on a distant diplomatic mission to the borders of China.

The following evening, the king visited the mansion unattended, intending to use his royal authority to win her favor.

The lady, perceiving the king’s intention, welcomed him with serene composure and royal hospitality. She invited him into the salon, seated him upon the sofa of honor, and served him a banquet consisting of twelve distinct dishes, each arranged in delicate porcelain bowls.

The king tasted the first dish; it was delicious. He tasted the second, third, and fourth dishes; each was seasoned differently with saffron, cinnamon, and rosewater, yet all possessed the same foundational texture.

'O fair lady,' asked the king, 'what are these twelve dishes you have prepared with such subtle art?'

The lady smiled with modest dignity and replied: 'Sire, though one is colored with yellow saffron, another with green herbs, and a third with pomegranate seeds, all twelve dishes are prepared from the exact same common fowl. In taste, nature, and nourishment, they are identical.'

The king, possessing a sharp intellect, perceived the profound allegory immediately: she was telling him that in the eyes of honor, one woman is like another, and that an honorable man does not leave his own table to rob the modest dish of his loyal soldier.

Ashamed of his unworthy impulse, the king rose from the sofa, slipped his royal signet ring beneath the cushion as a token of respect, and departed into the night without having uttered a single improper word.

When the husband returned, he noticed the royal ring and was troubled by suspicion. The king summoned the officer to court, promoted him to general of the imperial guard, and declared before all the emirs: 'Your garden was visited by the king, but its roses were guarded by a wall of virtue that no monarch could ever cross.' The household lived in honored prosperity, having conquered temptation with wit and moral majesty.
moral: Dignity, moral courage, and delicate wit can awaken the conscience of the most powerful ruler.
